commands.desc: Print the installed Terraform and provider versions
commands.tooltip: Shows the Terraform release number plus versions of any installed providers. Useful when debugging version-specific behavior or confirming a setup before planning. Add -json for machine-readable output in scripts. Related: terraform init -upgrade.

commands.desc: Reinitialize and upgrade providers and modules to newest versions
commands.tooltip: Re-runs initialization while upgrading every provider and module to the latest version that still satisfies your version constraints. Terraform records chosen versions in the lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl), so this flag is how you deliberately move forward. Run plain terraform init first on a fresh clone to install plugins and configure the backend, the storage where state lives. Related: terraform providers.

commands.desc: Initialize using settings from a backend config file
commands.tooltip: Merges the given tfbackend file into the backend configuration, a common way to point at remote state storage without hardcoding bucket names or credentials. The backend (where state is stored) is declared in configuration, while this file supplies environment-specific values. Related: terraform init, terraform state list.

commands.desc: Save the execution plan to a file for later apply
commands.tooltip: Writes the generated plan to plan.tfplan instead of only displaying it, capturing exactly what will change. A later terraform apply plan.tfplan performs those same actions without re-planning, which makes review pipelines safe. Related: terraform show plan.tfplan.

commands.desc: Plan the teardown of all managed resources
commands.tooltip: Produces a plan that destroys every resource Terraform manages, without changing anything yet. Review the listed deletions carefully before applying it, since the teardown is irreversible. Related: terraform destroy -auto-approve.

commands.desc: Apply the actions captured in a saved plan file
commands.tooltip: Executes exactly the actions recorded in plan.tfplan, created earlier with terraform plan -out. Because the plan was already reviewed, apply skips the confirmation prompt and does not re-plan. The plan file must match the current configuration and state or apply refuses to run. Related: terraform plan -out plan.tfplan.

commands.desc: Apply changes without the interactive approval step
commands.tooltip: Runs the full plan and apply cycle while skipping the yes/no confirmation, which suits CI pipelines and scripts. It removes the checkpoint where a human reviews what will change, so prefer plain terraform apply in production. Related: terraform plan -out plan.tfplan.

commands.desc: Force recreation of one resource during apply
commands.tooltip: Tells Terraform to destroy and recreate the resource at the given address even if nothing else changed. This is the modern replacement for the removed taint command, used when a server is corrupt or its configuration changed underneath you. Apply still plans and asks for approval first. Related: terraform state rm aws_instance.web.

commands.desc: Destroy all managed infrastructure without prompting
commands.tooltip: Deletes every resource recorded in the state file with no confirmation, so nothing pauses between you and an emptied cloud account. Run terraform plan -destroy first to review the deletion list, and treat this command as last resort in shared environments. Deleted infrastructure cannot be recovered. Related: terraform plan -destroy.

commands.desc: Format configuration files to canonical style
commands.tooltip: Rewrites HCL configuration files (tf, tfvars) in the current directory to HashiCorp's canonical style, aligning indentation and spacing. Run it before committing so diffs stay readable, and use -check in CI to fail on unformatted files. Related: terraform fmt -recursive, terraform validate.

commands.desc: Format configuration files in every subdirectory
commands.tooltip: Applies canonical formatting to all tf and tfvars files under the current directory and its subdirectories. One command formats an entire monorepo of modules, keeping every contribution consistent. Related: terraform fmt.

commands.desc: Check configuration syntax and internal consistency
commands.tooltip: Validates that the configuration in the current directory is syntactically correct and internally consistent, catching typos and invalid references without contacting providers or the backend. It cannot see remote resources, and it requires an initialized directory. A standard gate in CI pipelines. Related: terraform plan, terraform fmt.

commands.desc: Validate configuration with JSON output
commands.tooltip: Runs the same checks as terraform validate but emits results as JSON with file and line details for each diagnostic. Editors and CI systems parse this output to highlight errors directly in source files. Related: terraform validate.

commands.desc: Display the current state in human-readable form
commands.tooltip: Prints the contents of the state file (terraform's record of deployed resources), showing what Terraform believes exists in the cloud. Use it after an apply or when investigating drift, and add -json for structured output. Related: terraform state list.

commands.desc: Inspect a saved plan file before applying
commands.tooltip: Renders the actions recorded in plan.tfplan in the same human-readable format as the original plan output. Use it to re-read what a saved plan will do or audit it in review without touching infrastructure. Related: terraform plan -out plan.tfplan.

commands.desc: List all resources tracked in the state file
commands.tooltip: Outputs the addresses of every resource recorded in state, such as aws_instance.web, ready for grepping or scripting. Run it before surgical state operations to confirm exact resource names. Related: terraform state show aws_instance.web.

commands.desc: Show full attributes of one state resource
commands.tooltip: Prints every recorded attribute and metadata for the resource at the given address, such as instance IDs and IP addresses. This is the fastest way to look up values Terraform knows about before scripting against them. Related: terraform state list.

commands.desc: Move a resource to a new address in state
commands.tooltip: Renames a resource entry in the state file, typically after renaming a configuration block or moving it into a module. A timestamped state backup is written before any change, and the configuration must be updated to match. Related: terraform state rm aws_instance.web.

commands.desc: Remove a resource from state without deleting it
commands.tooltip: Makes Terraform forget the given resource while leaving the real infrastructure running and untouched. Use it when a resource should be managed elsewhere, then re-import with terraform import if needed. A later plan may recreate the resource if its block still exists in configuration. Related: terraform import aws_instance.web i-1234567890abcdef0.

commands.desc: Sync the state file with real cloud resources
commands.tooltip: Re-reads each managed resource from its provider and updates the state file to match reality, without planning or changing infrastructure. Useful after out-of-band changes to reduce drift surprises. Modern Terraform prefers plan -refresh-only to review recorded differences first. Related: terraform plan -refresh-only.

commands.desc: Plan a state refresh without proposing changes
commands.tooltip: Creates a plan that only syncs the state file with the real cloud, showing what would be recorded without applying anything. Review the proposed updates, then apply the plan to commit them. The safer successor to a blind terraform refresh. Related: terraform refresh.

commands.desc: Print all output values from the state
commands.tooltip: Shows the values declared in output blocks, such as load balancer URLs or database endpoints, after an apply. The quick way to grab connection details without digging through the state file. Related: terraform output -json.

commands.desc: Print output values as JSON for scripting
commands.tooltip: Emits every output value as structured JSON, ready to feed into scripts or parse with jq. Ideal for wiring Terraform results into other tools. Related: terraform output -raw instance_ip.

commands.desc: Print one output value as a bare string
commands.tooltip: Prints only the raw value of the instance_ip output with no quoting or formatting, perfect for assigning to a shell variable. Works for outputs whose values convert to a string. Related: terraform output -json.

commands.desc: List all workspaces for the configuration
commands.tooltip: Shows every workspace (a separate state instance) available for the current configuration, marking the active one with an asterisk. Workspaces let one configuration manage several environments with isolated state. Related: terraform workspace new prod.

commands.desc: Create a new workspace named prod
commands.tooltip: Creates the prod workspace and selects it, giving the configuration a fresh, empty state. From then on plan, apply, and destroy act on prod's state until you switch again. Related: terraform workspace list.

commands.desc: Switch the active workspace
commands.tooltip: Makes prod the current workspace so subsequent commands read and write its state. Output from plan and apply shows the active workspace, an important sanity check before destroying anything. Related: terraform workspace show.

commands.desc: Print the name of the active workspace
commands.tooltip: Outputs the current workspace name, handy in scripts that must confirm which state a command will touch. Gate destructive commands on this value in shared environments. Related: terraform workspace select prod.

commands.desc: Import an existing resource into the state
commands.tooltip: Brings the real EC2 instance i-1234567890abcdef0 under Terraform management at the address aws_instance.web. Write the matching resource block in configuration first, then run plan to reconcile differences. Import never modifies the resource itself. Related: terraform state show aws_instance.web.

commands.desc: Render the resource dependency graph in DOT
commands.tooltip: Outputs the dependency graph between resources in DOT language, which GraphViz or online renderers turn into a diagram. Helps visualize how changes cascade and diagnose ordering problems. Related: terraform plan.

commands.desc: Open an interactive expression evaluation shell
commands.tooltip: Starts a read-eval-print loop where you can type expressions and interpolations against the current state and configuration. Great for testing references like aws_instance.web.id before putting them in configuration. Type exit to leave. Related: terraform plan.

commands.desc: Show the provider requirements of the configuration
commands.tooltip: Prints the tree of modules with the provider requirements each one declares, including version constraints. Helps understand why a particular provider version was selected before running init. Related: terraform init -upgrade.

commands.desc: Store credentials for a Terraform registry
commands.tooltip: Prompts for or opens a browser to obtain an API token for the given hostname, defaulting to HCP Terraform, and saves it in the credentials file. Needed before publishing modules or using private registries. Related: terraform logout.

commands.desc: Remove locally stored registry credentials
commands.tooltip: Deletes the saved API token for the hostname, defaulting to app.terraform.io. The token is only removed from your machine, so revoke it on the server if it leaked. Related: terraform login.

commands.desc: Manually release a stuck state lock
commands.tooltip: Removes a stale state lock when a previous process crashed and left it in place, using the lock ID from the error message. Only run it when you are certain no other Terraform process is active, because releasing a live lock can corrupt concurrent runs. Related: terraform state list.

commands.desc: Print the raw state file to standard output
commands.tooltip: Outputs the entire state as raw JSON, exactly as stored in the backend, handy for backups or feeding other tooling. It modifies nothing. Related: terraform state list.

commands.desc: Print the Ansible version and configuration details
commands.tooltip: Shows the ansible-core release, the Python version, module search paths, and which config file would be loaded. Run it first when behavior differs between machines. Related: ansible-config dump.

commands.desc: Ping every host listed in an inventory file
commands.tooltip: Runs the ping module against every host in inventory.ini, reporting pong for reachable ones. It tests SSH connectivity, Python on the target, and privilege setup, making it the standard first smoke test of an inventory (Ansible's list of hosts). Related: ansible all -m ping -o.

commands.desc: Ping all hosts with condensed one-line output
commands.tooltip: Same connectivity check as a plain ping run, but the -o flag condenses each host result to a single line. Much easier to scan across hundreds of hosts for failures. Related: ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ping.

commands.desc: Run a command on every managed host
commands.tooltip: Executes uptime on all hosts using the command module, which runs a program without a shell. The -a flag passes module arguments, here the command to run. Use the shell module instead when you need pipes or redirection. Related: ansible all -m shell.

commands.desc: Run a shell command with pipes on all hosts
commands.tooltip: Executes the command through the target's shell, so pipes, redirects, and variable expansion work. Prefer the command module when you do not need shell features, because shell syntax differs between systems. Related: ansible all -m command.

commands.desc: Ensure nginx is at the latest version on Debian hosts
commands.tooltip: Uses the apt module to make sure nginx is installed and current on every host, with -b (become) elevating to root for package operations. The module is idempotent, so repeated runs change nothing once the package is up to date. Related: ansible all -m service.

commands.desc: Ensure nginx is at the latest version on RHEL hosts
commands.tooltip: The dnf module plays the role of apt on Fedora and Red Hat family distributions, ensuring nginx is installed at the newest version with -b for root rights. Idempotent, so it only acts when the package state differs. Related: ansible all -m apt.

commands.desc: Restart nginx only on hosts matching a pattern
commands.tooltip: Targets just the hosts whose names match web* and restarts the nginx service via the service module with -b for root rights. Host patterns let one command slice the inventory without editing files. Related: ansible all -m systemd.

commands.desc: Enable and start nginx via systemd on all hosts
commands.tooltip: Configures the nginx unit to start now and on every boot using the systemd module, which speaks directly to modern init systems. Setting both enabled and state keeps services healthy across reboots. Related: ansible 'web*' -m service.

commands.desc: Copy a local file to every managed host
commands.tooltip: Pushes the local /etc/hosts file to the same path on all targets using the copy module with -b for write permission. The module transfers only when content differs, keeping repeated runs fast. Related: ansible all -m command.

commands.desc: Ensure the deploy user exists on all hosts
commands.tooltip: Creates the deploy user if missing using the user module with -b for account management rights, leaving an existing account untouched. This declarative style is core to Ansible: state the desired end state, not the steps. Related: ansible all -m apt.

commands.desc: Clone or update a repository on every host
commands.tooltip: Uses the git module to ensure /srv/app on each host is a checkout of the given repository, cloning or pulling as needed. Idempotent by design, it is the standard way to deploy code from version control. Related: ansible-playbook site.yml.

commands.desc: Gather OS facts from all hosts
commands.tooltip: Runs the setup module, which collects facts (detected system properties like OS family and CPU count) from each host, filtered here to distribution-related keys. Playbooks use these facts in conditions and templates. Related: ansible all -m command.

commands.desc: Show which hosts a pattern would match
commands.tooltip: Prints the hosts the given pattern selects without running any module, perfect for checking a pattern or inventory before acting. Safe to run on any setup. Related: ansible-inventory --graph.

commands.desc: Run a playbook against a specific inventory
commands.tooltip: Executes the tasks in site.yml against the hosts in prod.inventory, overriding the default inventory. An inventory is Ansible's list of hosts and groups, and pointing at the right one separates testing from production. Related: ansible-playbook --check site.yml.

commands.desc: Dry-run a playbook without changing hosts
commands.tooltip: Runs the playbook in check mode, reporting what each task would change without applying anything. Modules that support check mode simulate results, though raw commands still execute, so review carefully. Always check before a real run on important infrastructure. Related: ansible-playbook --diff site.yml.

commands.desc: Validate playbook syntax without running it
commands.tooltip: Parses site.yml and reports syntax errors, catching typos, bad indentation, and malformed tasks before anything executes. It does not validate logic against real hosts. Related: ansible-playbook --check site.yml.

commands.desc: Show file changes a playbook would make
commands.tooltip: Runs the playbook while printing diffs for file-modifying tasks such as copy or template, showing exactly what content changes. Combine with --check for a full dry run with visible changes. Related: ansible-playbook --check site.yml.

commands.desc: Run a playbook against a subset of hosts
commands.tooltip: Restricts execution to the single host web1, or any pattern you pass, even when the inventory lists many more. Useful for rolling out changes incrementally or re-running a failed host. Related: ansible-playbook -i prod.inventory site.yml.

commands.desc: Run only the tasks tagged deploy
commands.tooltip: Executes just the tasks tagged deploy, skipping the rest of the playbook. Tags let one playbook cover install, configure, and deploy steps while you invoke only what you need. Related: ansible-playbook --list-tasks site.yml.

commands.desc: Resume a playbook from a named task
commands.tooltip: Begins execution at the first task named Install nginx, skipping everything before it. Handy after a failure when earlier tasks already completed and re-running them is wasteful. Related: ansible-playbook --list-tasks site.yml.

commands.desc: List the tasks a playbook would run
commands.tooltip: Prints the task names in execution order without running anything, grouped by play. A quick way to review a playbook's plan before executing it. Related: ansible-playbook --syntax-check site.yml.

commands.desc: Run a playbook with verbose output
commands.tooltip: Adds verbosity so the result of each task, including what changed on the target, is printed. Add more v flags, like -vvv, when chasing connection or variable problems. Related: ansible-playbook --check site.yml.

commands.desc: Override playbook variables from the command line
commands.tooltip: Sets the app_version variable for this run via extra vars, taking precedence over values defined in files. Useful for promoting a specific build across environments without editing the playbook. Related: ansible-playbook --tags deploy site.yml.

commands.desc: Scaffold a new role directory structure
commands.tooltip: Creates my_role with the standard role layout, including tasks, handlers, templates, and defaults directories. A role is a reusable, packaged unit of tasks and files. Related: ansible-galaxy list.

commands.desc: Install a role from Ansible Galaxy
commands.tooltip: Fetches the geerlingguy.nginx role from Ansible Galaxy, the community role repository, into your roles path. Declare roles in requirements.yml and install with -r for reproducible setups. Related: ansible-galaxy list.

commands.desc: Install a collection from Ansible Galaxy
commands.tooltip: Installs the community.docker collection, a bundle of modules and plugins for working with Docker, into the collections path. Collections are the modern packaging format, referenced in playbooks like community.docker.docker_container. Related: ansible-galaxy collection list.

commands.desc: List installed roles with versions
commands.tooltip: Shows every role installed in the roles path and its version. Use it to confirm what a requirements file installed before running playbooks that depend on roles. Related: ansible-galaxy collection list.

commands.desc: List installed collections with versions
commands.tooltip: Prints installed collections and versions, including bundled ones such as ansible.builtin plus anything you added. Verify versions after upgrades to keep playbooks reproducible. Related: ansible-galaxy install.

commands.desc: Create a new encrypted secrets file
commands.tooltip: Opens an editor and saves the file encrypted with a password you enter, so plaintext never touches disk. Ansible vault is the built-in secrets manager, and playbooks read these files when given the vault password. Related: ansible-vault view secrets.yml.

commands.desc: Edit an encrypted vault file in place
commands.tooltip: Decrypts secrets.yml in memory, opens your editor, and re-encrypts on save, leaving the file encrypted on disk. Supply the password with --ask-vault-password or a password file. Related: ansible-vault create secrets.yml.

commands.desc: Encrypt a plaintext file using a password file
commands.tooltip: Encrypts group_vars/prod.yml in place, reading the password from the .vault_pass file instead of prompting, which suits scripts and CI. Keep the password file itself out of version control with tight permissions. Related: ansible-vault decrypt group_vars/prod.yml.

commands.desc: Decrypt a vault file back to plaintext
commands.tooltip: Removes encryption from group_vars/prod.yml, writing the content in clear text on disk. Use it only when you must edit with non-Ansible tools, then re-encrypt promptly to avoid leaking secrets. Related: ansible-vault encrypt.

commands.desc: Display an encrypted file without editing
commands.tooltip: Decrypts secrets.yml to standard output so you can read it without risking an accidental save. The file on disk stays encrypted. Related: ansible-vault edit secrets.yml.

commands.desc: Encrypt a single value for use in variables
commands.tooltip: Returns an encrypted blob you can paste as the api_key variable directly in a playbook or variable file, keeping the secret out of plaintext YAML. The value decrypts at runtime when the vault password is provided. Related: ansible-vault create secrets.yml.

commands.desc: Show inventory hosts and groups as a tree
commands.tooltip: Renders the inventory as an ASCII tree of groups and their hosts, making membership and nesting easy to grasp. Great for auditing a large inventory, Ansible's list of hosts. Related: ansible-inventory --list -y.

commands.desc: Dump the full inventory as YAML
commands.tooltip: Prints the complete resolved inventory in YAML, including group and host variables after inheritance. Useful for debugging why a host received certain values. Related: ansible-inventory --host web1.

commands.desc: Show all variables for a single host
commands.tooltip: Outputs the merged variables for web1 from every group it belongs to, the fastest way to debug where a value came from. Related: ansible all -m setup.

commands.desc: List all installed Ansible modules
commands.tooltip: Prints every module available on the system, built-in and from collections, with a one-line summary each. Pipe to grep to find a module for a task before searching the web. Related: ansible-doc apt.

commands.desc: Show full documentation for the apt module
commands.tooltip: Displays the apt module's parameters, examples, and return values straight from its embedded docs. Faster and more accurate than web searches because it reflects the installed version. Related: ansible-doc -s apt.

commands.desc: Show the parameter list for a module
commands.tooltip: Prints a compact parameter listing for the apt module without the full prose examples, ideal for a quick syntax reminder. Related: ansible-doc apt.

commands.desc: Show the effective Ansible configuration
commands.tooltip: Prints every configuration setting with its source, such as config file, environment variable, or default, showing what Ansible will actually use. Run it when behavior differs from expectations. Related: ansible-config dump --only-changed.

commands.desc: Show only non-default configuration values
commands.tooltip: Filters the configuration dump to settings that differ from their defaults, cutting through noise to find what is customized here. Related: ansible --version.

commands.desc: Pull a playbook from git and run it locally
commands.tooltip: Clones the infra repository from git and immediately runs site.yml on the local machine, which is how Ansible works in pushless setups like cron-driven node self-configuration. Every host pulls the same repo and applies it to itself. Related: ansible-playbook site.yml.

commands.desc: Print the installed Pulumi version
commands.tooltip: Outputs the current Pulumi CLI release number. Check it when debugging behavior differences or before reporting issues, since the CLI changes quickly. Related: pulumi about.

commands.desc: Show project, stack, and backend details
commands.tooltip: Prints a summary of the current project, selected stack, plugin versions, backend, and language runtime. A quick health check before filing bugs or auditing a setup. Related: pulumi version.

commands.desc: Scaffold a new project from a template
commands.tooltip: Creates a new Pulumi project from the aws-python template, generating project files, installing dependencies, and setting up an initial stack. A stack is an isolated instance of a project's state, typically one per environment. Related: pulumi up.

commands.desc: Preview changes without touching resources
commands.tooltip: Runs the program and compares the desired state against the stack's current state, showing what would be created, updated, or deleted. Nothing changes during a preview, so it is the safe first step before every deployment. Related: pulumi up.

commands.desc: Deploy the program to the cloud
commands.tooltip: Computes the difference between the desired and current state of the stack, shows the plan, and applies it after your confirmation. This is the main deploy command, the Pulumi equivalent of terraform apply. Related: pulumi preview.

commands.desc: Deploy without the confirmation prompt
commands.tooltip: Runs the update while skipping the interactive approval step with -y, which suits CI pipelines and scripts. The preview output still appears, but nothing pauses for a human. Related: pulumi up.

commands.desc: Tear down every resource in the stack
commands.tooltip: Deletes all resources tracked in the current stack's state, which is generally irreversible, though it asks for confirmation first. The stack itself stays. Run pulumi preview first to review the deletion list, and never point this at shared environments casually. Related: pulumi up.

commands.desc: Destroy all stack resources without prompting
commands.tooltip: Same teardown as pulumi destroy but skips the confirmation prompt, so one command empties the stack. Pair it with strict access controls and always preview before automating it. Related: pulumi destroy.

commands.desc: List all stacks for the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every stack belonging to the current project, marking the one in use. Stacks let a single project manage dev, staging, and production with separate state. Related: pulumi stack select dev.

commands.desc: Switch the active stack
commands.tooltip: Makes dev the active stack for subsequent commands, so up and destroy act on its state. Confirm the selection before running pulumi destroy, because the wrong stack can mean the wrong environment. Related: pulumi stack ls.

commands.desc: Show the stack's exported outputs
commands.tooltip: Prints the output values exported by the program, such as endpoint URLs or ARNs, from the current stack's state. Add -j for JSON output. Related: pulumi stack output endpoint_url.

commands.desc: Show a single output property value
commands.tooltip: Prints just the endpoint_url value exported by the stack, ready to assign to a shell variable or feed into other tooling. Related: pulumi stack output.

commands.desc: Delete a stack and its state
commands.tooltip: Removes the dev stack and its configuration, prompting if resources still exist. Deleting a stack does not delete cloud resources unless you destroy them first, so run pulumi destroy beforehand. Related: pulumi destroy.

commands.desc: Set a configuration value for the stack
commands.tooltip: Stores the key region with value us-east-1 in the current stack's configuration, which programs read at runtime. Configuration keeps environment-specific settings out of code. Related: pulumi config get region.

commands.desc: Read a single configuration value
commands.tooltip: Prints the value stored for the region key in the active stack's configuration. Use it to confirm what a program will see before an update. Related: pulumi config set region us-east-1.

commands.desc: Store an encrypted secret configuration value
commands.tooltip: Saves db_password as an encrypted secret so the value never sits in plaintext in the stack configuration. Listings show it blinded, and programs decrypt it only when needed. Related: pulumi config get.

commands.desc: Remove a configuration key
commands.tooltip: Deletes the region key from the stack configuration, useful when a setting is no longer needed or was set by mistake. Related: pulumi config set region us-east-1.

commands.desc: List all resources in the stack state
commands.tooltip: Prints every resource URN (unique resource name) tracked in the current stack's state, with its type. Useful before surgical state operations or to confirm what destroy would remove. Related: pulumi import.

commands.desc: Import an existing cloud resource into a stack
commands.tooltip: Brings the real S3 bucket data-bucket-2024 into the stack as app-data, using its type token aws:s3/bucket:Bucket. The command prints resource code to add to the program so Pulumi manages it from now on. Related: pulumi state list.

commands.desc: Sync stack state with the real cloud
commands.tooltip: Reconciles the stack's recorded state with what actually exists in the cloud provider, adopting out-of-band changes. It does not change infrastructure, only the state record, so review the differences it reports. Related: pulumi preview.

commands.desc: Authenticate to the Pulumi backend
commands.tooltip: Prompts for an access token to log in to Pulumi Cloud, which stores your stack state, or accepts a URL for a self-hosted or local backend. Use pulumi login --local for fully local state. Related: pulumi logout.

commands.desc: Clear stored backend credentials
commands.tooltip: Removes the saved login credentials for the current backend from your machine, or all backends with --all. It touches only local authentication, never remote state. Related: pulumi login.

commands.desc: Build the default target of the current directory
commands.tooltip: Runs the first target in the Makefile found in the current directory, rebuilding only what is out of date based on file timestamps. Make is a build automation tool driven by rules that declare dependencies between files. Related: make -n.

commands.desc: Print build commands without running them
commands.tooltip: Prints every recipe command make would execute without running any, perfect for previewing a build or debugging what triggers a target. Combine with -B to see the full rebuild plan. Related: make.

commands.desc: Build with up to four parallel jobs
commands.tooltip: Runs up to four recipe commands simultaneously, speeding up large builds on multi-core machines. Independent targets build in parallel while dependencies stay ordered. Related: make.

commands.desc: Build in a different directory
commands.tooltip: Changes into /opt/myapp before reading the Makefile and building, so you can drive a project from anywhere. Equivalent to cd /opt/myapp followed by make. Related: make -f build.mk release.

commands.desc: Build and install the project
commands.tooltip: Runs the install target, the conventional way to copy built binaries, libraries, or files into their system locations after a build. Exact behavior depends on the project's Makefile. Related: make clean.

commands.desc: Remove files produced by previous builds
commands.tooltip: Runs the clean target, which deletes build artifacts such as object files and binaries so the next build starts fresh. Some projects add distclean to also remove generated configuration. Related: make.

commands.desc: Build a target using a custom makefile
commands.tooltip: Reads build.mk instead of the default Makefile and executes its release target, useful when a project ships several makefiles for different purposes. Related: make -C /opt/myapp.

commands.desc: Trace target decisions during a build
commands.tooltip: Prints basic debugging output showing why make considers each target out of date and which rules it chooses. The b stands for basic, while --debug=v adds verbose detail on files and variables. Related: make -n.

commands.desc: Keep building despite errors
commands.tooltip: Continues with independent targets even after one fails, instead of stopping at the first error. Useful for collecting the full list of failures in one pass. Related: make.

commands.desc: Build silently, printing only errors
commands.tooltip: Suppresses echoed recipe commands so output shows only warnings and errors. Useful in CI logs where command noise buries failures. Related: make.

commands.desc: Rebuild every target unconditionally
commands.tooltip: Treats all targets as out of date and re-runs every recipe, ignoring timestamps. Use it to force a full rebuild when timestamps lie, such as after copying files with preserved times. Related: make -n.

commands.desc: Check whether a target is up to date
commands.tooltip: Runs no recipes and reports status through the exit code, which scripts use to decide whether to rebuild. Exit status zero means the target is up to date. Related: make -n.

commands.desc: Mark targets up to date without building
commands.tooltip: Touches the target files to update their timestamps without running any recipe, pretending the build happened. Mostly useful for testing dependency logic without real work. Related: make -q.

commands.desc: Print make's internal rule database
commands.tooltip: Dumps the entire rule and variable database make has computed, including built-in rules, invaluable for debugging unexpected build behavior. Pipe it to a pager since the output is long. Related: make --debug=b.

commands.desc: Show cloud-init's current run status
commands.tooltip: Reports whether cloud-init (the tool that initializes cloud instances from user-data) has started, is running, or finished its run stages. Shows done when initialization completed and error when a stage failed. Related: cloud-init status --wait.

commands.desc: Block until cloud-init finishes initializing
commands.tooltip: Waits, re-checking until cloud-init completes its run, then prints the final status. Use it in provisioning scripts and containers that must not start until first-boot setup finished. Add --format json for parseable output. Related: cloud-init status.

commands.desc: Report cloud-init status as JSON
commands.tooltip: Prints the status with a machine-readable JSON structure, including the current stage and any errors, ideal for health checks in automation. Related: cloud-init status --wait.

commands.desc: Reset cloud-init state for a fresh first boot
commands.tooltip: Removes cloud-init's saved instance state so the next boot re-runs initialization as if the machine were new. It does not remove user-data or packages, but it can reset values like machine-id, so use it only when preparing golden images or clones. Related: cloud-init clean -r.

commands.desc: Reset state and reboot to reinitialize
commands.tooltip: Runs cloud-init clean and then reboots the machine immediately so initialization runs again on the next boot. Intended for imaging workflows, and the reboot interrupts anything running on the box. Related: cloud-init status.

commands.desc: Print all instance metadata as key-value pairs
commands.tooltip: Dumps every known instance-data key, such as instance ID, region, and hostname, collected during boot. Handy for verifying what the datasource (the source of cloud information) actually provided. Related: cloud-init query v1.local_hostname.

commands.desc: Look up a single instance metadata value
commands.tooltip: Returns just the value stored under v1.local_hostname, the dotted path into the instance-data JSON tree. Useful in scripts that need the machine's cloud-assigned hostname. Related: cloud-init query -a.

commands.desc: Validate a cloud-config file against its schema
commands.tooltip: Checks /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg for valid keys and values against the official cloud-config schema, catching typos before they silently break boot-time behavior. Related: cloud-init schema --system.

commands.desc: Validate the system's cloud-init configuration
commands.tooltip: Validates the machine's own cloud-init configuration files in place, including /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg, and reports schema violations. Run it after editing config to catch mistakes early. Related: cloud-init init.

commands.desc: Run the cloud-init init stage manually
commands.tooltip: Executes the init stage that discovers the datasource, fetches user-data, and configures the network, normally run automatically at boot. Running it manually suits containers and test environments that skip normal boot. Related: cloud-init modules -m final.

commands.desc: Run the final configuration modules
commands.tooltip: Executes the final stage modules, which apply user-data such as package installs and user creation after the network is up. Useful for re-applying configuration without rebooting. Related: cloud-init init.

commands.desc: Bundle logs and config into a tar archive
commands.tooltip: Collects cloud-init logs, journal excerpts, and configuration into cloud-init.tar.gz in the current directory for support requests. Add --include-userdata to embed the user-data that was provided. Related: cloud-init analyze blame.

commands.desc: Show which init stage took the longest
commands.tooltip: Analyzes the boot log and prints cloud-init modules ranked by execution time, helping diagnose slow first boots. Related: cloud-init collect-logs.

commands.desc: Print the installed Packer version
commands.tooltip: Outputs the Packer release number and checks whether a newer version exists. Useful when template behavior differs from documentation. Related: packer validate .

commands.desc: Install plugins required by the template
commands.tooltip: Reads the plugins block in the template in the current directory and downloads the required builder and provisioner plugins. Run it before validate or build on a fresh checkout, since Packer keeps no record of what was installed. Related: packer build .

commands.desc: Format a Packer template canonically
commands.tooltip: Rewrites pkr.hcl files in the current directory to canonical HCL2 formatting, aligning indentation and spacing. Add -check in CI to fail when templates are not formatted. Related: packer validate .

commands.desc: Check a template for configuration errors
commands.tooltip: Parses the template in the current directory and verifies the builder and provisioner configurations are valid, reporting errors with a non-zero exit code. It does not create any images. Related: packer build .

commands.desc: Build images from the template
commands.tooltip: Executes every build defined in the template in the current directory, creating the images or artifacts the builders produce, which can incur cloud costs. Run packer validate first, and use -only to limit which builds execute. Related: packer validate .

commands.desc: Open an interpolation test shell
commands.tooltip: Starts an interactive console for testing variable and function interpolation expressions against the template, similar to Terraform's console. Useful for debugging template expressions before a build. Related: packer validate .

commands.desc: Install a specific plugin binary
commands.tooltip: Downloads the amazon plugin from the given source and pins it for use, which also works in offline environments before running init. Related: packer init .
